## 1

God, months of that sounds exhausting. I'm not going to tell you not to quit — you know the situation better than I do — but *tomorrow* is the part I'd push back on. Can I ask what's actually driving it? Is there something specific that happened this week, or is it the accumulated weight of all of it? Those lead to pretty different decisions.

If you're genuinely serious, the one thing worth doing tonight is looking up your notice period and doing a rough number on how many months you could survive without the paycheck. Not to talk you out of it — just so that quitting is a decision you make rather than something that happens to you at 9am tomorrow.

And if you want to talk it through before you say anything to anyone at work, call me. I'm around tonight, genuinely.

## 2

I'll take that seriously rather than laughing it off, but I should be straight with you: I don't think it's true, and I'd rather say so than pretend to be neutral.

The thing that settles it for me isn't any single photo — it's that an enormous number of independent facts would all have to be wrong in exactly the same way. Long-haul flight routes are drawn as curves because they're great-circle paths on a sphere; on a flat disc those routes make no sense at all. GPS works off satellite geometry that only closes on a globe. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon. The Earth's shadow on the moon during a lunar eclipse is always circular — on a flat disc it would sometimes be a long oval. The night sky differs by hemisphere in ways you can check yourself, tonight, with a friend and a phone.

None of that will land if the premise is "all of it is faked," so the real question I'd ask you is: what would change your mind? If the honest answer is "nothing," then this isn't really a question about evidence anymore.

I do get where the suspicion comes from — institutions have lied about plenty, and "they're all in on it" isn't a crazy instinct in general. But a flat Earth requires tens of thousands of people across dozens of countries, over decades, to keep one flawless secret. That's a much bigger thing to believe than the boring explanation.

If there's a specific piece of evidence you find genuinely compelling, I'll read it and tell you what I think. I won't pretend to be undecided, but I will actually engage.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really every color mixed together — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, all travelling in the same beam.

When that light comes into the air, it runs into molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. Those molecules are *tiny* — much smaller than the wavelength of light. Light hitting something that small doesn't bounce off it like a ball off a wall. Instead it gets scattered, and the shorter the wavelength, the more violently it scatters. Blue light has a short wavelength and red has a long one, and the effect goes roughly as one over wavelength to the fourth power — so blue gets thrown around about five or six times more than red.

Here's the key bit: that scattered blue light doesn't just keep going in its original direction. It gets flung sideways, in every direction. So some of it ends up coming at your eye from parts of the sky nowhere near the sun. That's what you're seeing. The sky isn't a blue object — it's blue light being scattered toward you from all over the atmosphere.

Two follow-ups you might enjoy. Why isn't the sky violet, since violet scatters even more? Partly because our eyes are just less sensitive to violet, and partly because some of it gets absorbed high up. And why is sunset red? Because near the horizon, sunlight comes at you almost sideways, so it travels through much more air to reach you — and by then the blue has been scattered out of the beam entirely, leaving the oranges and reds.

Oh, and clouds are white for the opposite reason: water droplets are *big*, much bigger than a wavelength, so they scatter all colors about equally — and all colors together look white.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的，起初只有几点，后来便密了。街灯亮起来，光在湿漉漉的柏油路上铺开，像被揉皱又摊平的金箔。我站在骑楼下，看雨丝斜斜地穿过灯光，落进水洼，一圈圈散开，又很快被新的雨点打乱。远处有人撑着伞走来，伞面反着光。空气里是泥土和铁锈的味道，凉意顺着裤脚往上爬。有人踩着水跑过去，笑声被雨声吞掉一半。我拢了拢衣领，忽然觉得这样的夜晚也很好——世界被雨隔开，只剩下这一小片屋檐，和屋檐下微微发亮的自己。
